'''Grigory Mikhailovich Rodchenkov''' ({{langx|ru|Григорий Михайлович Родченков}}; born 24 October 1958) is a former head of [[Moscow antidoping laboratory|Russia's national anti-doping laboratory]], the ''Anti-Doping Center''. Rodchenkov is known for his involvement in the [[Doping in Russia|state-run doping program in Russia]].

In November 2015, the Independent Commission of the [[World Anti-Doping Agency]] (WADA) determined Rodchenkov was "at the heart of the positive drug test coverup", and that he had been directly involved with concealing positive tests and destroying 1,417 urine samples.<ref name="WADA2015" /> Rodchenkov made headlines in 2016 after an interview to ''[[The New York Times]]'' exposing the doping program in Russia. Rodchenkov said he developed a three-drug cocktail of banned substances that he mixed with liquor and provided to dozens of athletes at the [[2014 Winter Olympics|Sochi Olympics]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/13/sports/russia-doping-sochi-olympics-2014.html|title=Russian Insider Says State-Run Doping Fueled Olympic Gold|last1=Ruiz|first1=Rebecca R.|date=12 May 2016|work=The New York Times|access-date=8 December 2017|last2=Schwirtz|first2=Michael|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Rodchenkov's allegations were confirmed by the independent [[McLaren Report]], leading to Russia's partial bans from the [[2016 Summer Olympics]] and [[2018 Winter Olympics]]. Since the revelations became public, Rodchenkov has been living in hiding, under [[witness protection]].<ref>{{Cite news|date=31 July 2020|title=The Russian whistleblower hiding from the Kremlin's spies|language=en-GB|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/stories-53596997|access-date=31 July 2020}}</ref>

Rodchenkov and his connections to Russian doping were the subject of the 2017 [[Netflix]] documentary ''[[Icarus (2017 film)|Icarus]]'', which won the [[Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature]] at the [[90th Academy Awards|90th Oscars ceremony]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=McNary|first=Dave|date=5 March 2018|title=Netflix Wins First Feature Documentary Oscar With 'Icarus'|url=https://variety.com/2018/film/awards/oscars-icarus-best-documentary-feature-film-1202717030/|access-date=31 July 2020|website=Variety|language=en}}</ref>

In 2023, the United States authorized the ''Rodchenkov Act'' which seeks to identify and sanction individuals involved in doping at major international sporting events if American companies are involved in sponsoring those events or the American financial system is utilized by the organizers.<ref>{{cite web |title=The United States' Response to the Russian Doping Scandal |url=https://scholarship.law.marquette.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1815&context=sportslaw |website=Marquette Law Scholarly Commons}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.outsideonline.com/health/training-performance/rodchenkov-act-doping/|title=This Could Be a Game Changer in the Fight Against Doping|date=13 October 2023|author=Ian Dille}}</ref>

== Life and career ==
Rodchenkov was born in Moscow. His mother worked as a doctor at Kremlin Hospital (now [[Central Clinical Hospital]]). Throughout school he was involved in athletics and during his studies he was a member of the MSU national team and met the standard of the Master of Sports in Athletics.<ref>{{Cite news|last=|first=|date=2 August 2020|title='The Kremlin wants me dead': Russia's sports doping whistleblower speaks out|language=en-GB|work=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/aug/02/the-kremlin-wants-me-dead-russias-sports-doping-whistleblower-speaks-out|access-date=29 March 2021|issn=}}</ref> Rodchenkov graduated from Moscow State University and received his PhD in chemistry with a focus on chemical kinetics and catalysis. In 1985, he started working at the Moscow Anti-Doping Centre.<ref>{{Cite web|last1=Mosko|first1=Alexey|last2=RBTH|date=16 May 2016|title=Olympic doping scandal: Whistleblower Rodchenkov may face court in Russia|url=https://www.rbth.com/sport/2016/05/16/olympic-doping-scandal-whistleblower-rodchenkov-may-face-court-in-russia_593539|access-date=1 April 2021|website=www.rbth.com|language=en-US}}</ref> In 1986, he worked at the 1986 Goodwill Games in Moscow and co-discovered 14 positive samples, including those of sprinter [[Ben Johnson (Canadian sprinter)|Ben Johnson]]. However, the announcement was not made because the sports and party leaders of the [[Soviet Union|USSR]] did not want to cause a scandal.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ahmed |first1=Murad |title=Whistleblower Grigory Rodchenkov: 'Sport won't be clean. Never' |url=https://www.ft.com/content/0630521e-37d3-4a44-a7ea-b2dc82f8bad9 |access-date=13 August 2021 |work=www.ft.com |date=31 July 2020}}</ref> 

Rodchenkov later described the Soviet Union's state-sponsored doping program served as a model for Russia's program in the 21st century, with Vladimir Putin merely continuing what Joseph Stalin started.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rferl.org/a/the-1980-moscow-olympics-rank-as-the-cleanest-in-history-athletes-recall-how-the-u-s-s-r-cheated-the-system-/30741567.html |title=The 1980 Olympics Are The 'Cleanest' In History. Athletes Recall How Moscow Cheated The System. |last1=Aleksandrov |first1=Alexei |last2=Aleksandrov |first2=Grebeniuk |last3=Runets |first3=Volodymyr |publisher= |date=22 July 2020 |website=Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty |access-date=26 December 2021}}</ref> In 1994, he moved to Interlab.<ref name="SII-2017">{{Cite web|date=20 November 2017|title=Russian State doping may go back to Soviet era|url=https://www.sportsintegrityinitiative.com/russian-state-doping-may-go-back-soviet-era/|access-date=22 April 2021|website=Sports Integrity Initiative|language=en-GB}}</ref> When he returned to Russia, he worked for different petrochemical companies.{{Failed verification|date=June 2021}} He joined the Anti-Doping Centre in [[Calgary]] for the [[1988 Winter Olympics]].<ref name="SII-2017" /> From July 2006 until November 2015 he worked as the director of the ''Anti-Doping Center'', then Russia's only laboratory accredited by [[World Anti-Doping Agency|WADA]].<ref>{{cite news |title=10 facts about Grigory Rodchenkov (In Russian: 10 фактов о Григории Родченкове) |url=https://www.sport-express.ru/doping/reviews/999332/ |work=Sport-Express |date=13 May 2016}}</ref>

=== Doping investigation in 2011 ===

In 2011, Russian authorities opened an investigation against Rodchenkov's sister, champion runner {{ill|Marina Rodchenkova|ru|Родченкова, Марина Михайловна}}, for buying and possessing banned drugs that she admitted she had intended to supply to athletes.<ref name="WADA2015" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.netflix.com/title/80168079|title=Icarus {{!}} Netflix Official Site|website=www.netflix.com|access-date=8 December 2017}}</ref> Rodchenkov was also arrested in relation to this investigation and questioned on suspicion of sourcing and selling banned drugs.<ref name="WADA2015" /> He was placed in a psychiatric hospital for [[schizotypal personality disorder]] following a suicide attempt after charges were filed against him.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://meduza.io/en/feature/2017/12/05/a-certifiable-charlatan|title='A certifiable charlatan' What Russia has to say about Grigory Rodchenkov, the whistleblower who may have tanked Moscow's 2018 Olympic hopes|publisher=Meduza|date=5 December 2017|accessdate=27 February 2023}}</ref> Charges against him were eventually dropped, but his sister was convicted in December 2012 and given a suspended sentence.<ref name="WADA2015" /><ref name="Championat">{{cite web|title=Все мозги разбил на части. Родченков спасся от тюрьмы в психушке|url=https://www.championat.com/other/article-247594-otkuda-vzjalos-kriminalnoe-proshloe-grigorija-rodchenkova-i-psihbolnica.html|date=13 May 2016|access-date=6 December 2017|archive-date=6 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171206202004/https://www.championat.com/other/article-247594-otkuda-vzjalos-kriminalnoe-proshloe-grigorija-rodchenkova-i-psihbolnica.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="NewsruMarina">{{cite news|title=Сестру директора антидопинговой лаборатории осудили за сбыт допинга|url=http://www.newsru.com/sport/12apr2013/rodch.html|agency=[[NEWSru]]|date=12 April 2013}}</ref>

At the time, Rodchenkov was the director of Russia's national anti-doping laboratory. In June/July 2013, British journalist Nick Harris informed the [[International Olympic Committee]] (IOC) and [[World Anti-Doping Agency|WADA]] about this criminal drug case and suspicions of Rodchenkov's involvement, but this information was apparently ignored.<ref name=SpInt160725/> Rodchenkov claims he was not jailed by Russian authorities in 2012 because they had earmarked him to dope their athletes at the [[2014 Winter Olympics]] in [[Sochi]].<ref name=BBC160719 />

=== Doping scandal after 2014 ===

In 2015 the WADA Independent Commission (IC) made numerous accusations against Rodchenkov.<ref name="WADA2015">{{cite web |title= Independent Commission Investigation |url=https://www.wada-ama.org/sites/default/files/resources/files/wada_independent_commission_report_1_en.pdf |publisher= WADA|date=9 November 2015 |access-date=3 January 2020}}</ref> The IC established Rodchenkov "not only accepted, but also requested money" from athletes in order to conceal their positive test results. "Rodchenkov had personally instructed and authorized the disposal of 1,417 samples" prior to the arrival in Moscow of a WADA audit team, which "directly defied and violated the WADA directives".{{citation needed|date=August 2021}} In addition, "Rodchenkov instructed that all records showing the existence of the samples, as well as any documentation of the resulting analysis, be destroyed." Rodchenkov later admitted he destroyed the samples on purpose in order to limit the extent of WADA's audit. The IC report concluded Rodchenkov was "at the heart of the positive drug test coverup".

Shortly after release of the IC report, WADA suspended the Moscow Antidoping Center, which Rodchenkov had headed since 2006.<ref name=DW151110/> In January 2016, fearing for his safety, Rodchenkov boarded a flight from Moscow to Los Angeles. He settled in the United States and entered the [[witness protection]] program.<ref>{{cite web |author1= Ronald Katz |title= 'Icarus': Best Film Based on a Doping Scheme (but the Wrong One) |url=https://www.thenation.com/article/icarus-best-film-based-on-a-doping-scheme-but-the-wrong-one/ |publisher= TheNation |access-date= 21 January 2020 |ref= TheNation2018 |date= 14 March 2018 |archive-date= 17 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190417132835/https://www.thenation.com/article/icarus-best-film-based-on-a-doping-scheme-but-the-wrong-one/ |url-status= dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.cnn.com/2017/11/29/sport/russia-doping-whistleblower-grigory-rodchenkov-winter-olympics-ioc/index.html|title=Doping whistleblower urges Russia to come clean|first=David |last= Stokes|work= CNN|access-date=8 December 2017}}</ref> Two major Russian anti-doping executives, Vyacheslav Sinev and Rodchenkov's friend Nikita Kamaev, unexpectedly died in the months after the doping scandal started.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/news/world/russian-anti-doping-official-dies-suddenly-article-1.2532985|title= Second former Russian anti-doping official dies suddenly|work=NY Daily News|access-date=8 December 2017|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.vedomosti.ru/politics/news/2016/02/15/629425-skonchalsya-direktor-rossiiskogo-antidopingovogo|title=Внезапно скончался бывший исполнительный директор Российского антидопингового агентства|last=Ведомости|date=15 February 2016|access-date=11 May 2018|trans-title=The former executive of Russian anti-doping agency suddenly dies}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cbc.ca/sports/nikita-kamaev-leading-russian-anti-doping-official-was-planning-on-writing-a-book-before-sudden-death-1.3457433|title= Russian anti-doping official planned book before sudden death - CBC Sports|access-date= 27 December 2017}}</ref>

Rodchenkov discussed doping at the Sochi Olympics with whistle-blower [[Doping_in_Russia#2010–2014:_allegations_of_state-sponsored_doping_and_2014_ARD_documentary|Vitaly Stepanov]], who recorded 15 hours of their conversations without Rodchenkov's knowledge.<ref name=CBS60Min/> Rodchenkov also gave details to ''[[The New York Times]]'', alleging that Russia's [[Federal Security Service]] (FSB, previously [[KGB]]) was involved in covering up positive doping samples.<ref name=NYT160512/> In July 2016, the [[McLaren Report]], an independent investigation commissioned by WADA, found corroborating evidence after conducting witness interviews, reviewing thousands of documents, cyber analysis of hard drives, forensic analysis of urine-sample collection bottles, and laboratory analysis of individual athlete samples, with "more evidence becoming available by the day".<ref name=WADA160718/> The Moscow laboratory "operated under State oversight and control" and "personnel were required to be part of the State directed system that enabled Russian athletes to compete while engaging in the use of doping substances."<ref name=IOCLegkov/>

On 9 December 2016 [[Richard McLaren (academic)|McLaren]] published the second part of his independent report. The investigation found that from at least 2011 to 2015, more than 1,000 Russian competitors in various sports (including summer, winter, and Paralympic sports) benefited from the cover-up.<ref name=NYT161209>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/12/09/sports/russia-doping-mclaren-report.html |title= Russia's Doping Program Laid Bare by Extensive Evidence in Report |work= The New York Times |first= Rebecca R. |last= Ruiz |date= 9 December 2016 }}</ref><ref name=Guardian161209>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2016/dec/09/mclaren-report-into-doping-in-sport-part-two-live |title=McLaren report: more than 1,000 Russian athletes involved in doping conspiracy |work=The Guardian |first=Lawrence |last=Ostlere |date=9 December 2016 }}</ref> Emails indicate they included five blind powerlifters, who may have been given drugs without their knowledge, and a fifteen-year-old.<ref name=AP161213>{{cite news |url=https://apnews.com/8be9cb7fcb5b4d65b1031597bb9f9e5e/Emails-show-how-Russian-officials-covered-up-mass-doping |title= Emails show how Russian officials covered up mass doping |first= James |last= Ellingworth |work= [[Associated Press]] |date= 13 December 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161214061329/https://apnews.com/8be9cb7fcb5b4d65b1031597bb9f9e5e/Emails-show-how-Russian-officials-covered-up-mass-doping |archive-date= 14 December 2016 |url-status= live }}</ref>

According to McLaren's summary of the evidence provided by Rodchenkov, a key aspect of the doping scheme was the creation and use of a so-called "Sochi Duchess List". This list contained the names of 37 Russian athletes "whose samples were to be automatically swapped for their own clean urine stored in the FSB Command Center at Sochi". Those athletes' samples needed to be swapped because the athletes "had been authorised to use the cocktail of [[oxandrolone]], [[methenolone]] and [[trenbolone]] during the Games".<ref name="CAS-Legkov">{{cite web |title= Arbitration CAS 2017/A/5379 Alexander Legkov v. International Olympic Committee, award of 23 April 2018 |url=https://jurisprudence.tas-cas.org/Shared%20Documents/5379.pdf |access-date=3 January 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Axon |first=Rachel |title=More than 1,000 Russian athletes involved in doping, McLaren report says|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/olympics/2016/12/09/more-than-1000-russian-athletes-involved-doping-mclaren-report-says/95187710/|access-date=28 April 2021|website=USA TODAY |language=en-US}}</ref> The Russian Olympic Committee insists the Duchess List is nothing more than a competition schedule, which was prepared ahead of the Sochi Games for the purpose of identifying potential medallists.{{cn|date=November 2023}}

During arbitration between [[Alexander Legkov]] and the International Olympic Committee (IOC), the IOC submitted that "Dr. Rodchenkov's account of events is truthful and accurate", stating:
* Since Dr Rodchenkov is no longer in Russia, he is now able to speak honestly with less fear of the consequences than if he had chosen to describe the existence and detail of the scheme while he was in Russia. 
* Dr Rodchenkov's statements are precise and clear. They are also very consistent and contain "no contradictions" among the various elements of his account. 
* Dr Rodchenkov provided detailed information concerning particular athletes only when he appears to have specific information relating to those athletes. In many cases, he simply mentions the athlete's presence on the Duchess List and the objective consequence of this, without seeking to add specific details.
* On every occasion when other evidence has been available, that evidence has "systematically corroborated" Dr Rodchenkov's account.<ref name="CAS-Legkov"/>

According to the IOC, minor inconsistencies in his testimony were considered unimportant. For example, the Duchess Cocktail which he developed was originally described in writing as a mixture of trenbolone, oxandrolone, and methasterone; it was subsequently described as containing metenolone, not methasterone. Rodchenkov stated the word "methasterone" in the original was a "typographical error".<ref name="CAS-Legkov"/>

Rodchenkov stated he personally had never distributed the Duchess Cocktail, had never seen an athlete take the mixture or instruction being given either to athletes or to coaches to use the substance, and had never seen an athlete give a clear urine sample or "tamper with a doping sample".<ref name="CAS-Legkov"/>{{rp|70}} Rodchenkov also stated: (a) he "never observed first hand any bottles being opened or de-capped"; (b) accordingly, he did not know the "precise method" used to open the bottles; but (c) he did see a "table with instruments that resembled a dentist's tools".<ref name="CAS-Legkov"/>

According to the Arbitral Award in the arbitration between Alexander Legkov, Russia and the IOC, Rodchenkov's statement is called "a bare assertion which is uncorroborated by any contemporaneous documentary evidence. As such, the probative weight of this evidence is limited and the Panel is unable to find based on such evidence that the Athlete committed an ADRV" (anti-doping rule violation).<ref name="CAS-Legkov"/>

== Reactions ==
Following the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi, Russian President [[Vladimir Putin]] awarded Rodchenkov the [[Order of Friendship]].<ref name=NYT160512 /> In 2016, after the doping allegations were widely reported, Putin called Rodchenkov a "man with a scandalous reputation".<ref name=BBC160719 />

The McLaren Report stated Rodchenkov was "an integral part of the conspiracy to extort money from athletes in order to cover up positive doping test results."<ref name="WADA2015" /> It also found that Rodchenkov was truthful with respect to the subject matter under investigation.<ref name=IOCLegkov />

In November 2017, an IOC panel concluded: "Whatever his motivation may be and whichever wrongdoing he may have committed in the past, Dr Rodchenkov was telling the truth when he provided explanations of the cover-up scheme that he managed".<ref name=AP171127 /><ref name=IOCLegkov />

On 5 December 2017, it was announced Russia would compete as [[Olympic Athletes from Russia at the 2018 Winter Olympics|Olympic Athletes from Russia]] under a neutral flag at the 2018 Winter Olympics.<ref name="Hobson-2017">{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/russia-banned-from-2018-olympics-following-doping-allegations/2017/12/05/9ab49790-d9d4-11e7-b859-fb0995360725_story.html|title=Russia banned from 2018 Olympics for widespread doping program|last=Hobson |first=Will|date=5 December 2017|newspaper=Washington Post|access-date=18 December 2017|language=en-US|issn=0190-8286}}</ref> Following the announcement, [[James "Jim" Walden|Jim Walden]], an attorney for Rodchenkov, issued a statement applauding the decision by the IOC that sends "a powerful message that it will not tolerate state-sponsored cheating by any nation".

<blockquote>As the world has seen, Dr Rodchenkov provided credible and irrefutable evidence of the Russian state-sponsored doping system," Walden said in a statement. "Russia's consistent denials lack any credibility, and its failure to produce all evidence in its possession only further confirms its high-level complicity.<ref name="Hobson-2017" /></blockquote>

Russia's doping program and Rodchenkov's work were highlighted in testimony before the [[Commission on Security and Cooperation in Europe|U.S. Helsinki Commission]] (also known as the Commission on Security and Cooperation in Europe) in Washington, DC, on 22 February 2018. During that hearing, [[Jim Walden (lawyer)|Walden]] discussed Rodchenkov's work in detail and suggested the World Anti-Doping Agency and the International Olympic Committee needed to do more to restore integrity to international sport.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.c-span.org/video/?441528-1/attorney-speaks-russias-doping-program|title=Attorney Speaks Russia's Doping Program, Feb 22 2018 {{!}} Video |publisher=C-SPAN|language=en-US|access-date=23 February 2018}}</ref>

Despite the information presented in the McLaren Report, Russia was reinstated by the [[International Olympic Committee|IOC]] after the conclusion of the 2018 Games. In an editorial published in the American newspaper USA Today, Rodchenkov expressed his dismay at the decision, calling it "catastrophic".<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/olympics/2018/09/18/grigory-rodchenkov-wada-decision-reinstate-russia-catastrophic/1347844002/|title=Opinion: Decision to reinstate Russia would be catastrophic in fight against doping|work=USA TODAY|access-date=4 October 2018|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/olympics/2018/09/18/grigory-rodchenkov-wada-decision-reinstate-russia-catastrophic/1347844002/|title=Opinion: Decision to reinstate Russia would be catastrophic in fight against doping|work=USA TODAY|access-date=24 September 2018|language=en}}</ref> His lawyer, [[Jim Walden (lawyer)|Jim Walden]], issued a statement on behalf of Rodchenkov saying the decision to reinstate Russia is "the greatest treachery against clean athletes in Olympic history".<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.chicagotribune.com/sports/international/ct-spt-russia-anti-doping-agency-20180920-story.html|title=Despite protests, Russia's anti-doping agency reinstated|last=Pells|first=Eddie|work=chicagotribune.com|access-date=24 September 2018|language=en-US}}</ref> Rodchenkov continues to fear for his life and remains in hiding under protective custody.<ref>[https://open.spotify.com/episode/15p3DpjZeaXCwcXyGTytMj Joe Rogan Podcast Episode 1592 with Bryan Fogel]</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Russian Doping Whistleblower Says He Fears For His Life|url=https://www.npr.org/2017/12/27/573870686/russian-doping-whistleblower-says-he-fears-for-his-life|access-date=7 May 2021|website=NPR.org|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title=Whistleblower suspected British doping|language=en-GB|work=BBC Sport|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/42723660|access-date=7 May 2021}}</ref>

===In Russia===
Russian state-owned news agency TASS reported that sports minister [[Pavel Kolobkov]] said the investigative committee found no evidence to support the state operated a doping system. That committee seeks Rodchenkov's extradition from the United States, where he is in witness protection. Despite assertions from Russian officials that no system existed, "empirical evidence is totally to the contrary", IOC member [[Dick Pound]] said, adding, "so I think what we're seeing in the Russian press is for domestic consumption".<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/olympics/2017/11/14/doping-scandal-wada-decide-whether-russia-compliance-code/861306001/|title=Doping scandal: WADA to decide whether Russia is in compliance with code|date=14 November 2017|work=USA Today|access-date=14 November 2017|language=en}}</ref>

=== Lawsuit by Mikhail Prokhorov ===
Following Russia's banning from the 2018 Winter Olympics and the stripping of medals from multiple Russian athletes, Russian oligarch [[Mikhail Prokhorov]], at the time the controlling owner of the [[Brooklyn Nets]] basketball team, agreed to finance a defamation lawsuit in New York against Rodchenkov.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://nypost.com/2018/02/20/russian-olympians-file-libel-suit-against-doping-whistleblower/|title=Russian Olympians file libel suit against doping whistleblower|date=20 February 2018|work=New York Post|access-date=2 May 2018|language=en-US}}</ref> The suit claims Rodchenkov defamed three Russian biathletes — [[Olga Zaitseva|Olga Zaytseva]], [[Yana Romanova]] and [[Olga Vilukhina]] — when Rodchenkov included them on a list of athletes who took performance-enhancing drugs as part of a state-controlled program that corrupted the 2014 [[2014 Winter Olympics|Winter Olympics in Sochi]], Russia. The women, who were stripped of the silver medal they won as part of a relay team, are seeking $10 million each in damages.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/02/20/sports/olympics/russia-doping-prokhorov.html|title=N.B.A. Owner Backs Lawsuit Against Russian Doping Whistle-Blower|last=Panja|first=Tariq|date=20 February 2018|work=The New York Times|access-date=2 May 2018|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

In April 2018, Rodchenkov, through his lawyer, [[Jim Walden (lawyer)|Jim Walden]], countersued Prokhorov under New York's [[Strategic lawsuit against public participation|anti-SLAPP]] law, claiming that Prokhorov's suit was frivolous and intended to limit individuals from exercising their [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]] rights to free speech.<ref name="NYT-2018">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/04/30/sports/prokhorov-rodchenkov-russia-doping.html|title=Doping Whistleblower Sues Russian Olympians and Their Oligarch Backer, an N.B.A. Owner|date=30 April 2018|work=The New York Times|access-date=2 May 2018|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> According to published reports, the countersuit is likely to seek the names of other individuals who are financing the lawsuit against Rodchenkov as well as information about the assets of Prokhorov.<blockquote>"Prokhorov has assets here," Walden said. "We need to go about expeditiously securing them, so he doesn't go about taking them out of the country. You can expect that's what we're going to be looking at next."<ref name="NYT-2018" /></blockquote>Walden stated that he believes Prokhorov's lawsuit was intentionally designed to uncover Rodchenkov's whereabouts in the United States and allow agents of the Russian government to find him.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://themoscowtimes.com/news/russian-doping-whistleblower-counter-sues-athletes-tycoon-prokhorov-61309|title=Russian Doping Whistleblower Counter-sues Athletes, Russian Tycoon|access-date=2 May 2018|language=en}}</ref>

== ''Icarus'' ==
Rodchenkov was featured in the 2017 Netflix documentary ''[[Icarus (2017 film)|Icarus]]'', directed by [[Bryan Fogel]]. In ''Icarus'', Rodchenkov describes his involvement in a conspiracy to help Russian athletes to beat doping tests in the Olympic Games.<ref name="usatoday20170805">{{cite web|last1=Ryan|first1=Patrick|title=Netflix's wild documentary 'Icarus' exposes Russian doping scandal|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/life/movies/2017/07/31/icarus-netflix-documentary-russian-doping-scandal/523785001/|website=USA Today|access-date=5 August 2017}}</ref> On 4 March 2018, ''Icarus'' won an [[Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature]].

== William Hill Sports Book of the Year ==
Rodchenkov was the 2020 winner of the [[William Hill Sports Book of the Year]] for his book ''The Rodchenkov Affair: How I Brought Down Putin's Secret Doping Empire''. He was, however, unable to collect the £30,000 prize money as he has been placed under a witness protection scheme in the United States.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Ingle|first=Sean|date=3 December 2020|title=Russian doping whistleblower wins William Hill Sports Book of Year|language=en-GB|work=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2020/dec/03/russian-doping-whistleblower-grigory-rodchenkov-wins-william-hill-sportsbook-of-year-russian-doping-scandal|access-date=4 January 2021|issn=0261-3077}}</ref>
